summary: Shows how the AES Galois Counter Mode can provide both confidentiality and data integrity in the SSH transport layer. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo shows how to protect an SSH session with a single algorithm that both encrypts the data and checks that it has not been changed. It works out the keys, the starting value and the packet layout that the two ends need to agree on.

questions: how does gcm work in ssh
how does aes gcm work in ssh
why is the ssh packet length not encrypted with gcm
subtitle: Using one algorithm to encrypt an SSH session and to prove the data was not altered.

tldr.problem: SSH encrypts its traffic and checks its integrity with separate algorithms, which costs extra work on both ends of every connection.
tldr.mechanism: The document shows how AES Galois Counter Mode can be used inside the SSH transport layer, with the packet length passed as additional authenticated data and a 12-octet nonce that carries a counter incremented for every packet.
tldr.outcome: Two algorithm names are added for SSH, one with a 128-bit key and one with a 256-bit key, both producing a full 16-octet authentication tag that may not be truncated.

facts.label: Authentication tag
facts.value: 16 octets, and may not be truncated

facts.label: Random padding length
facts.value: At least 4 and at most 255 octets

today: RFC 5647 is an Informational memo published in August 2009, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It records an approach to using AES-GCM inside SSH and states that the two algorithm names it describes were added to the SSH encryption algorithm and MAC algorithm registries.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Galois Counter Mode (GCM) is a mode of operation for block ciphers that provides both confidentiality and data integrity. GCM encrypts with counter mode, an operation that can be efficiently pipelined, and its authentication uses operations that are particularly well suited to implementation in hardware, which makes it appealing for high-speed implementations or for implementations in a compact circuit.

The purpose of the document is to show how GCM with either AES-128 or AES-256 can be integrated into the Secure Shell Transport Layer Protocol, defined in RFC 4253. The stated reason is efficiency: using AES-GCM to provide both confidentiality and data integrity is generally more efficient than using two separate algorithms to provide these security services.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo shows how to protect an SSH session with one algorithm that both encrypts the data and checks that it has not been altered.

sections.title: Properties of Galois Counter Mode
sections.content:
An authenticated encryption with GCM takes four inputs: the plain text, which is both authenticated and encrypted; the additional authenticated data, which is authenticated but not encrypted; the initialisation vector; and the block cipher key. It produces two outputs: the cipher text and an authentication tag. The initialisation vector is called the nonce in RFC 5116.

Authenticated decryption takes the cipher text, the additional authenticated data, the authentication tag, the initialisation vector and the block cipher key. It returns a failure indicator if the authentication tag is invalid, and returns the plain text if and only if the tag is valid. AES-GCM is prohibited from returning any portion of the plain text until the authentication tag has been validated. That feature greatly simplifies the security analysis of any system using AES-GCM, but it creates an incompatibility with the requirements of secure shell, which the document returns to later.

For a given block cipher key, it is critical that no initialisation vector is used more than once, and the document explains how that goal is achieved in secure shell.
sections.plainLanguage: The encryption produces a tag, a short value that lets the receiver tell whether the data was altered. The receiver hands back the data only when the tag checks out. Reusing the same starting value with the same key would break that guarantee, so the memo tracks it carefully.

sections.title: Review of Secure Shell
sections.content:
The goal of secure shell is to establish two secure tunnels between a client and a server, one carrying client-to-server traffic and the other carrying server-to-client traffic. Each tunnel is encrypted, and a message authentication code is used to ensure data integrity.

The tunnels are initialised by the secure shell key exchange protocol, which negotiates a mutually acceptable set of cryptographic algorithms and produces a secret value K and an exchange hash H shared by the client and server. The initial value of H is saved as the session identifier. A hash-based key derivation function is then applied to K to generate the required symmetric keys, with each tunnel getting a distinct set: the initialisation vector for each direction is derived with the letters A and B, the encryption key with C and D, and the integrity key with E and F.

If AES-GCM is selected as the encryption algorithm for a tunnel, AES-GCM must also be selected as the message authentication code algorithm, and the other way round. Because an AEAD algorithm uses the encryption key to provide both confidentiality and data integrity, the separate integrity key is not used with AES-GCM. Either the server or the client may at any time request that the session be rekeyed, which updates K, H and all the derived symmetric keys, while the session identifier stays the same.

After the key exchange, all further traffic is parsed into secure shell binary packets: a four-octet packet length, a one-octet padding length, the payload, the random padding and the MAC. The authentication tag produced by AES-GCM goes in the MAC field at the end of the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: SSH derives separate keys for each direction of the connection. Each packet carries its length, a padding length, the payload, some random padding and a code for checking integrity. With this cipher the tag takes the place of that last field, and the separate integrity key is no longer needed.

sections.title: AES GCM Algorithms for Secure Shell
sections.content:
Two algorithm names are defined. AEAD_AES_128_GCM uses an AES key length of 16 octets, and AEAD_AES_256_GCM uses 32 octets. Because of the format of secure shell binary packets, the buffer sizes needed to implement them are smaller than those required in RFC 5116.

For both algorithms the maximum plain text length is 2^32 - 32 octets, the maximum additional authenticated data length is 4 octets, the nonce length is fixed at 12 octets for both the minimum and the maximum, and the maximum cipher length is 2^32 octets.

Both algorithms produce a 16-octet authentication tag, which RFC 5116 calls a message authentication code. Some applications allow a truncated version of this tag, but that is not allowed in AES-GCM secure shell: all implementations must use the full 16-octet tag.
sections.plainLanguage: Two versions are offered, one with a 128-bit key and one with a 256-bit key. Both use a 12-byte starting value and both produce a 16-byte check value, which may not be shortened.

sections.title: Processing Binary Packets in AES-GCM Secure Shell
sections.content:
The 12-octet initialisation vector is broken into two fields: a four-octet fixed field and an eight-octet invocation counter, which is treated as a 64-bit integer and incremented after each invocation of AES-GCM to process a binary packet. The key stream comes in blocks of 16 octets, produced by encrypting a 16-octet structure made of the same fixed field and invocation counter followed by a four-octet block counter. The block counter starts at one and is incremented as each block of key is produced. SSH also requires the data to be encrypted to be padded out to a multiple of the block size, which is 16 octets for AES-GCM.

The inputs to the authenticated encryption are the padding length, the payload and the random padding as plain text; the packet length as additional authenticated data; the initialisation vector as described above; and the encryption key formed during the key exchange. The random padding must be at least 4 octets and at most 255 octets, and the total length of the plain text must be a multiple of 16 octets. The binary packet that is sent is the four-octet packet length, the cipher text and the 16-octet authentication tag.

The packet length field cannot be encrypted. Section 6.3 of RFC 4253 requires the packet length, padding length, payload and padding to be encrypted, but that would deadlock: the tag cannot be verified until the packet is parsed, the packet cannot be parsed until the packet length has been decrypted, and the packet length cannot be decrypted until the tag has been verified. The resolution is to treat the packet length as additional authenticated data rather than as plain text. The field is therefore not encrypted, but it is covered by the tag. This violates the requirements of RFC 4253, and the document discusses the consequences in its security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: The starting value carries a counter that rises with every packet, so each packet is encrypted with a fresh value. The length of a packet is left visible but is still covered by the check value, because SSH and this cipher cannot both encrypt the length and verify the check value before reading it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations in RFC 4251 apply.

RFC 4253 requires that forming the authentication tag involve the packet sequence number, a 32-bit value that counts the binary packets sent on a given tunnel. Since the sequence number is, up to an additive constant, the low 32 bits of the invocation counter, the presence of the invocation counter in the initialisation vector does ensure that the sequence number is involved in forming the tag, though this involvement differs slightly from the requirements in Section 6.4 of RFC 4253.

Leaving the packet length unencrypted is the other consequence of the decision described above. In theory one could argue that encrypting the whole binary packet makes the secure shell data flow a featureless octet stream. In practice the flow arrives in bursts, with the length of each burst strongly correlated to the length of the underlying binary packets, so encrypting the packet length does little to disguise that length. Secure shell already has two other mechanisms that mask structure in the underlying plain text stream far more effectively than encrypting the packet length does: random padding and SSH_MSG_IGNORE messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Two points are checked. The packet count is tied to the tag, so a packet cannot be replayed unnoticed. The visible packet length is judged to leak little, because traffic already arrives in bursts and SSH pads it.

data.title: Secure shell binary packet
data.code:
uint32    packet_length;  // 0 <= packet_length < 2^32
byte      padding_length; // 4 <= padding_length < 256
byte[n1]  payload;        // n1 = packet_length-padding_length-1
byte[n2]  random_padding; // n2 = padding_length
byte[m]   mac;            // m  = mac_length

viz.caption: THE 12-OCTET NONCE USED FOR EVERY PACKET (RFC 5647, FIGURE 3)

fields.name: Fixed field
fields.desc: Four octets that stay the same for the session.

fields.name: Invocation counter
fields.desc: Eight octets treated as a 64-bit integer, incremented after each packet.
